desc:
You are given two strings a and b. Pick a non-empty subsequence x of a and a non-empty subsequence y of b and look at the concatenation x + y. Return the largest possible length of such a concatenation that is a palindrome, or 0 if no choice gives a palindrome.

For example, a = "cacb" and b = "cbba" give 5 (take x = "ab" and y = "cba", giving "abcba"), a = "ab" and b = "ab" give 3 ("aba"), and a = "xy" and b = "zz" give 0.
constraints: a and b consist of lowercase English letters
hints: Glue the two strings into one string s = a + b. A palindromic subsequence of s that uses letters from both halves is exactly what you are after.
Compute dp[i][j], the length of the longest palindromic subsequence of s[i..j], with the usual recurrence.

The two outermost letters of the final palindrome are s[i] from a and s[j] from b, with s[i] == s[j]. Whenever i lies in a, j lies in b and the letters match, dp[i][j] is a candidate, because both sides are then guaranteed to be used.
editorial: Let s = a + b. A subsequence of s splits into a part taken from a followed by a part taken from b, so we need a palindromic subsequence of s that has at least one letter on each side of the boundary. The longest palindromic subsequence DP gives dp[i][j] for every interval.

A palindromic subsequence that takes letters from both parts has a first letter inside a (position i) and a last letter inside b (position j) which are equal. Exactly in that situation we must use the matched pair: for every i < |a| ≤ j with s[i] == s[j], the value dp[i][j] (which equals 2 + dp[i+1][j-1]) is achievable and uses both parts, hence it is a candidate for the answer. Take the maximum of all candidates, or 0 if there are none.

Why it is enough: the best valid palindrome has outer letters at some positions i and j as described, and inside them it is any palindromic subsequence of s[i+1..j-1], at best dp[i+1][j-1]. The table has O((|a|+|b|)2) cells, so time and space are quadratic in the total length.
